label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
If a knot $K$ in the 3-sphere $S^3$ has a nontrivial Jones polynomial
$V_K(t)$ and $\operatorname{span} V_K(t) \le 14$, then $K$ does not
admit purely cosmetic surgery.
head: environment

label: prop:braid-index
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:braid-index}
Let $K$ be a knot in $S^3$ with Jones polynomial $V_K(t)$.
If $br(K) \le 4$ and $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)$ is odd, then $K$
admits no purely cosmetic surgery.
head: environment

label: lem:6throot
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lickorish--Millett \cite[Theorem 3]{LM86}, we have
\[
V_K(\zeta_6)=\pm(i\sqrt3)^d,
\]
where $d=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3} H_1( \Sigma_2(K) ; \mathbb{F}_3 )$ and
$\Sigma_2(K)$ is the double branched cover of $S^3$ along $K$.
On the other hand, $H_1(\Sigma_2(K);\mathbb{Z})$ is a finite group of order $\vert\Delta_K(-1)\vert=\det(K)$ (see \cite{Lickorish}).
Since $V_K(-1)=\Delta_K(-1)=1$ (see \cite{Jones}), this order is $1$, and so $H_1(\Sigma_2(K);\mathbb{Z})=0$.
Hence $d=0$, and $V_K(\zeta_6)=\pm1$.

To determine the sign of $V_K(\zeta_6)$, we prepare the following claim.

\begin{claim}\label{clm:congruence}
For any Laurent polynomial $f(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm1}]$, we have
\[
f(\zeta_6)\equiv f(-1) \pmod{1+\zeta_6}.
\]
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Since $\zeta_6-(-1)=1+\zeta_6$, we have $\zeta_6\equiv -1 \pmod{1+\zeta_6}$.
First, let $k\ge 0$.
Multiplying the congruence $\zeta_6\equiv-1$ by itself $k$ times, we have $\zeta_6^k\equiv(-1)^k$.
Next, let $k<0$.
Take an integer $j$ with $6j+k\ge0$.
Since $\zeta_6^6=1$ and $6j$ is even, we have
\[
\zeta_6^k=\zeta_6^{6j+k}\equiv(-1)^{6j+k}=(-1)^k .
\]
Thus $\zeta_6^k\equiv(-1)^k \pmod{1+\zeta_6}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Now write $f(t)=\sum_k a_k t^k$ with $a_k\in\mathbb{Z}$, where the sum is finite.
Then
\[
f(\zeta_6)=\sum_k a_k\zeta_6^k\equiv\sum_k a_k(-1)^k=f(-1) \pmod{1+\zeta_6}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

By Claim~\ref{clm:congruence} and the assumption $V_K(-1)=1$, we have
\[
V_K(\zeta_6)\equiv V_K(-1)=1 \pmod{1+\zeta_6}.
\]

If $V_K(\zeta_6)=-1$, then $-1\equiv1 \pmod{1+\zeta_6}$, which contradicts Claim~\ref{clm:norm} below.

\begin{claim}\label{clm:norm}
The element $1+\zeta_6$ does not divide $2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_6]$.
In other words, $-1\not\equiv 1 \pmod{1+\zeta_6}$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
We have
\[
N(1+\zeta_6)=(1+\zeta_6)(1+\overline{\zeta_6})=2+(\zeta_6+\overline{\zeta_6})=3, \qquad N(2)=4 .
\]
If $1+\zeta_6$ divided $2$, then $N(1+\zeta_6)=3$ would divide $N(2)=4$, which is a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Therefore $V_K(\zeta_6)=1$.

head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The condition $d=0$ alone does not determine the sign of $V_K(\zeta_6)$.
For example, the figure-eight knot $4_1$ with $\det(4_1)=5$ and the knot $5_2$ with $\det(5_2)=7$ both have $d=0$,
but they satisfy $V_{4_1}(\zeta_6)=V_{5_2}(\zeta_6)=-1$.
These values are consistent with Claim~\ref{clm:congruence}:
we have $V_{4_1}(\zeta_6)-V_{4_1}(-1)=-1-5=-6$ and $V_{5_2}(\zeta_6)-V_{5_2}(-1)=-1-(-7)=6$.
Both are divisible by $3$, and hence by $1+\zeta_6$, since $3=(1+\zeta_6)(1+\overline{\zeta_6})$ and $1+\overline{\zeta_6}\in\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_6]$.

label: prop:conditions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:conditions}
Suppose that a knot $K \subset S^3$ admits purely cosmetic surgery.
Then the Jones polynomial $V_K(t)$ of $K$ must satisfy the following conditions:
\begin{align*}
  \text{(A1)} \quad & V_K(1)      = 1, \\
  \text{(A2)} \quad & V_K'(1)     = 0, \\
  \text{(A3)} \quad & V_K''(1)    = 0, \\
  \text{(A4)} \quad & V_K'''(1)   = 0, \\
  \text{(A5)} \quad & V_K''''(1)  = 0,
\end{align*}
and also the following conditions at roots of unity:
\begin{align*}
  \text{(E2)} \quad & V_K(\zeta_2)=1, \\
  \text{(E3)} \quad & V_K(\zeta_3)=1, \\
  \text{(E4)} \quad & V_K(\zeta_4)=1, \\
  \text{(E5)} \quad & V_K(\zeta_5)=1, \\
  \text{(E6)} \quad & V_K(\zeta_6)=1.
\end{align*}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The conditions (A1)--(A5) and (E3)--(E5) follow from
\cite[Sections 2 and 3]{ichihara2026purelycosmeticsurgeriesknots}.
By \cite[Corollary 1.4]{DLME}, we have $\Delta_K(t)=1$, and hence
$V_K(-1)=\Delta_K(-1)=1$.
Thus (E2) holds, and Lemma~\ref{lem:6throot} gives (E6).
Here, since $V_K(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm1}]$, each of the conditions (E3)--(E6) does not depend on the choice of the primitive root of unity:
if $V_K(\xi)=1$ for one primitive $m$-th root of unity $\xi$, then $V_K(\xi')=1$ for every primitive $m$-th root of unity $\xi'$, since $\xi'$ is a Galois conjugate of $\xi$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The conditions (A1), (A2) and (E3) hold for every knot in $S^3$ (see \cite{Jones, Lickorish}).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The proof above actually shows that $\operatorname{span} V_K(t) \ge 16$ in the case $r \le 0 \le s$. 
Thus, if a knot $K$ admitting purely cosmetic surgery satisfies $\operatorname{span} V_K(t) = 15$, then the degrees of the non-zero terms of $V_K(t)$ are either all positive or all negative.
head: environment

label: prop:span15-PCScandidate
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:span15-PCScandidate}
Suppose that a knot $K\subset S^3$ admits purely cosmetic surgery and
$\operatorname{span} V_K(t)=15$.
Then there exists a unique integer $r\ge1$ such that
\[
V_K(t)=G_r(t)\qquad\text{or}\qquad V_K(t)=G_r(t^{-1}).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As shown in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, the conditions
(A1)--(A5) and (E2)--(E6) imply $Q(t)\mid(V_K(t)-1)$.
Moreover, $V_K(t)\ne1$ since $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)=15$.
We can therefore write
\[
V_K(t)=1+Q(t)h(t),\qquad h(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm1}].
\]
As observed in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, if $r \le 0 \le s$, where $r$ (resp. $s$) is the lowest (resp. highest) degree of a non-zero term of $V_K(t)$, then
\[
\operatorname{span} V_K(t)\ge16.
\]
Hence, under the assumption $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)=15$, the degrees of the non-zero terms of $V_K(t)$ are either all positive or all negative.

Suppose first that all non-zero terms have positive degrees.  In this case, we have $r\ge1$.
Since $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)=15$, the highest degree is $r+15$.
As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, we have $h(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t]$.
Multiplying $V_K(t)=1+Q(t)h(t)$ by
$-1/Q(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt^n$ and rearranging, we obtain
\[
h(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt^n
      -V_K(t)\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt^n
\]
as an identity of formal power series.
Since $V_K(t)$ has no terms of degree less than $r$ and the
series $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt^n$ has only non-negative powers of $t$,
the product on the right has no terms of degree less than $r$.
Thus the coefficient of $t^n$ in $h(t)$ is $a_n$ for $0\le n<r$.
Moreover, comparison of the highest degrees in $V_K(t)=1+Q(t)h(t)$ gives
\[
r+15=16+\deg h,
\]
and therefore
\[
\deg h=r-1.
\]
Thus $h(t)$ has no terms of degree greater than $r-1$.
Together with the coefficient comparison above, this gives
\[
h(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}a_jt^j.
\]
Thus $V_K(t)=G_r(t)$.

If all non-zero terms of $V_K(t)$ have negative degrees, then $V_K(t^{-1})$ has only positive-degree terms and still satisfies
\[
Q(t)\mid(V_K(t^{-1})-1),\qquad \operatorname{span} V_K(t^{-1})=15,
\]
by the identity $t^{16}Q(t^{-1})=-Q(t)$.  The lowest degree of a non-zero term of $V_K(t^{-1})$ is $-s\ge1$.
Applying the preceding case to $V_K(t^{-1})$, we obtain
$V_K(t)=G_{-s}(t^{-1})$.

Finally, for each $r\ge1$, the lowest degree of a non-zero term of
$G_r(t)$ is $r$, and the highest degree of a non-zero term of
$G_r(t^{-1})$ is $-r$.
Thus the integer in the statement is uniquely determined by $V_K(t)$,
since all its non-zero terms have either positive or negative degrees.

label: rem:census19
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:census19}
Using Burton's Regina census \cite{BurtonKnots}, we performed a computer-assisted search for prime knots through $19$ crossings.
No prime knot in this range has Jones polynomial
\[
V_K(t)=G_r(t)\qquad\text{or}\qquad V_K(t)=G_r(t^{-1})
\]
for any $r\ge1$.
Note that the purely cosmetic surgery conjecture itself has been verified for all knots with at most $19$ crossings by Futer, Purcell and Schleimer \cite[Theorem 2.11]{FPS}.
The search above concerns a different question, namely, whether the polynomials $G_r(t)$ and $G_r(t^{-1})$ are realized as Jones polynomials of knots, regardless of purely cosmetic surgery.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, to the contrary, that $K$ admits purely cosmetic surgery.
Note that, since $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)$ is odd, we have $V_K(t)\ne1$, and so $K$ is nontrivial.
Thus, by Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, we have $\operatorname{span} V_K(t)\ge15$.
Also, by Daemi--Lidman--Miller Eismeier \cite[Corollary 1.4]{DLME}, a nontrivial knot admitting purely cosmetic surgery has
\[
g(K)=2,\qquad \Delta_K(t)=1.
\]

Since $K$ is nontrivial, if $br(K)\le2$, then $K$ is a $(2,p)$-torus knot, and Moser's classification of surgeries on torus knots implies that $K$ admits no purely cosmetic surgery \cite{Moser}.
By Varvarezos \cite{Varvarezos}, a nontrivial knot which is the closure of a $3$-braid does not admit purely cosmetic surgery.
Hence we have $br(K)=4$, that is, $K$ is the closure of a $4$-braid $\beta$.
Let $e=e(\beta)$ be its exponent sum.

Regard the closure of $\beta$ as a transverse knot in the standard tight contact structure on $S^3$.
Its self-linking number is
\[
\operatorname{sl}(\widehat{\beta})=e-4.
\]
By Bennequin's inequality \cite{Bennequin}, applied using a minimal-genus Seifert surface for $K$, we have
\[
e-4=\operatorname{sl}(\widehat{\beta})
\le 2g(K)-1=3.
\]
Let $\beta^*$ be the $4$-braid obtained from $\beta$ by replacing each generator $\sigma_i$ by $\sigma_i^{-1}$.
Then $\widehat{\beta^*}$ is the mirror image of $K$ and $e(\beta^*)=-e$.
Since the Seifert genus is invariant under taking mirror images,
\[
g(\widehat{\beta^*})=g(K)=2.
\]
Applying Bennequin's inequality to the transverse closure of $\beta^*$ gives
\[
-e-4=\operatorname{sl}(\widehat{\beta^*})
\le 2g(\widehat{\beta^*})-1=3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|e|\le7.
\]

For a knot which is the closure of a $4$-braid of exponent sum $e$, the Jones--Alexander relation for closed $4$-braids (\cite[Theorem 5]{Stoimenow4braid}, \cite[Proposition 11.11]{Jones87}) gives 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:four-braid-relation}
\begin{aligned}
&t^{-e}V_K(t)+t^eV_K(t^{-1})\\
&\quad=
\left(t^{-3/2}+t^{-1/2}+t^{1/2}+t^{3/2}\right)
\left(t^{-e/2}+t^{e/2}\right)
-
\left(t^{-2}+t^{-1}+2+t+t^2\right)\Delta_K(t).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Since $\Delta_K(t)=1$ and $|e|\le7$, the degrees occurring in the first product on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:four-braid-relation} lie in $[-5,5]$, while those occurring in the second term lie in $[-2,2]$.
Hence all non-zero terms on the right-hand side have degrees in $[-5,5]$.

Let $r$ (resp. $s$) be the lowest (resp. highest) degree of a non-zero term of $V_K(t)$, and set $N:=s-r=\operatorname{span} V_K(t)$.
Then the lowest and the highest degrees of the non-zero terms of the two summands on the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:four-braid-relation} are
\[
r-e,\ s-e
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
e-s,\ e-r,
\]
respectively.
In particular, the highest degrees of the two summands are $s-e$ and $e-r$, whose sum is $N$.  Thus
\[
M:=\max\{s-e,\,e-r\}\ge \frac{N}{2}\ge\frac{15}{2}.
\]
Since $M$ is an integer, we have $M\ge8$.
Moreover, the two highest degrees cannot be equal, since their sum $N$ is odd.
Hence the term of degree $M$ on the left-hand side comes from exactly one of the two summands and has a non-zero coefficient.
This contradicts the fact that all non-zero terms on the right-hand side have degrees in $[-5,5]$.
Therefore $K$ admits no purely cosmetic surgery.
